#1
L: If more-excellent than-action, in-your-view, [is] wisdom, O Janārdana — then why into-terrible action me do-you-urge, O Keśava?
I: Arjuna said: If wisdom is better than action in your eyes, Janārdana, why then do you urge me into this dreadful action, Keśava?
N: Arjuna reopens the question chapter 2 seemed to have closed. Cet karmaṇaḥ te matā buddhir, 'if wisdom is, in your view, better than action', refers back to 2.49-51's ranking of buddhi-yoga above ordinary action; Arjuna reads that teaching as an argument for withdrawal, which the rest of this chapter corrects. Janārdana ('rouser of men') and Keśava (traditionally 'slayer of the demon Keśin') are two more epithets of Kṛṣṇa, alongside the many already used in chapter 2.
#2
L: With-speech that-seems-confused you-seem-to-bewilder my understanding; that one-thing tell, having-decided-for-certain, by-which the-better I-might-attain.
I: Your words seem to confuse me and bewilder my understanding. Tell me for certain the one thing by which I may attain what is truly best.
N: Vyāmiśreṇa iva vākyena, 'with speech that seems confused', and mohayasi iva, 'you seem to bewilder', repeat iva twice in one line — Arjuna feels, rather than flatly asserts, that Kṛṣṇa is contradicting himself. The vulgate reads vyāmiśreṇeva (vyāmiśreṇa + iva, 'as if confused'); the BORI critical edition reads vyāmiśreṇaiva instead (vyāmiśreṇa + eva, 'indeed confusing, indeed mixed'), a real difference in sense — eva asserts what iva only suggests.
#3
L: In-this world a-twofold path, formerly, [was] declared by-me, O sinless-one: by-the-yoga-of-knowledge, for-the-Sāṃkhyas; by-the-yoga-of-action, for-the-yogins.
I: The Blessed Lord said: In this world I have taught, from of old, a twofold path: for the followers of Sāṃkhya, the yoga of knowledge, and for those who practice yoga, the yoga of action.
N: Kṛṣṇa answers Arjuna's confusion by naming, for the first time explicitly, the two paths already distinguished in substance at 2.39: jñāna-yoga, associated with the Sāṃkhyas, and karma-yoga, with the yogins. Sāṃkhya is named here as a proper term and kept untranslated per convention, alongside dharma, yoga, brahman and the guṇas; this chapter goes on to argue that karma-yoga, not withdrawal from action, is what a man in Arjuna's position needs (verses 4-8 give the reason why total inaction is not even possible).
#4
L: Not by-non-undertaking of-actions freedom-from-action does-a-man attain; nor by-renunciation-alone perfection does-he-reach.
I: A man does not attain freedom from action merely by abstaining from action, nor does he reach perfection by renunciation alone.
N: Naiṣkarmya, 'the state of action-lessness' (from niṣ-karma), names the goal Arjuna implicitly wants after chapter 2; the verse denies that simply not acting (anārambhāt), or formally renouncing (saṃnyasanāt), gets one there. This opens the section (through verse 8) arguing that action itself is unavoidable.
#5
L: For not anyone, even-for-a-moment, ever remains non-action-doing; everyone is-made-to-act, powerless, by-the-guṇas born-of-nature.
I: No one can remain, even for a moment, without acting; everyone is driven to act, powerless to stop, by the guṇas born of nature.
N: The reason behind verse 4's denial: action is not optional at all. Prakṛti-jair guṇaiḥ, 'by the guṇas born of nature (prakṛti)', is the poem's first mention of the three guṇas, kept untranslated per convention and developed at length in chapter 14; avaśaḥ, 'powerless, not his own master', underscores that even the wish to stop acting cannot succeed.
#6
L: The-organs-of-action having-restrained, who sits, with-the-mind dwelling-on the-objects-of-the-senses — whose-self-is-deluded, of-false-conduct, he is-called.
I: One who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in his mind on the objects of the senses — his mind confused, he is called a hypocrite.
N: This verse names the wrong response to verses 4-5: karma-indriyāṇi, 'the organs of action' (hands, feet, speech and so on, as distinct from the organs of perception, a distinction assumed but not spelled out here), can be restrained while the mind still dwells (smaran) on the sense-objects. Mithyācāraḥ, 'one of false conduct', is the poem's word for this kind of outward-only restraint — hypocrisy.
#7
L: But-who, [his] senses with-the-mind having-restrained, undertakes the-yoga-of-action with-the-organs-of-action, O Arjuna, unattached — he excels.
I: But the man who controls his senses with his mind, Arjuna, and, unattached, engages the organs of action in the discipline of action — he is superior.
N: The positive counterpart to verse 6's hypocrite: the same restraint (niyamya, from the same root as saṃyamya in verse 6) is applied first to the mind, so that the organs of action can then be used, unattached (asaktaḥ), for karma-yoga itself — outward action joined to inward detachment, rather than outward inaction hiding inward craving.
#8
L: The-prescribed action do, you; action [is] better, indeed, than-inaction; even the-maintenance-of-your-body would-not-be-accomplished without-action.
I: Perform the action that is your duty, for action is better than inaction; even the upkeep of your own body would be impossible without acting at all.
N: Kṛṣṇa's first direct command to act: niyatam karma, 'the prescribed action', i.e. one's own duty (sva-dharma, named explicitly at verse 35). Śarīra-yātrā, 'the body's journey', a vivid compound for day-to-day bodily upkeep, makes the argument concrete: total inaction is not even physically possible. The Wikisource text reads na prasiddhyed akarmaṇaḥ, with a doubled dh (from the root sidh/sidhyati, 'to succeed'); the BORI critical edition reads na prasidhyed akarmaṇaḥ, with a single dh, the more regular form of the verb, with no difference of sense.
#9
L: Except-for-action-done-for-the-sake-of-sacrifice, this world [is] bound-by-action; for-that-purpose action, O son-of-Kuntī, free-from-attachment, perform!
I: This world is bound by action, except for action performed as sacrifice. Do your work for that purpose, Kaunteya, free from attachment.
N: Yajña, 'sacrifice', begins the chapter's extended treatment (through verse 16) of ritual sacrifice as the paradigm case of unattached action: an act done not for private gain but to sustain a larger order escapes karma-bandhana, 'the bondage of action'. Mukta-saṅgaḥ, 'free from attachment', restates verse 7's asaktaḥ in different words.
#10
L: Together-with-sacrifice creatures having-created, formerly said Prajāpati: 'By-this shall-you-multiply; this to-you let-it-be the-yielder-of-desired-wishes.'
I: In ancient times, Prajāpati, having brought forth creatures together with sacrifice, said: 'By this may you prosper; let this be the cow that grants your desires.'
N: Prajāpati, the Vedic creator-deity ('lord of creatures'), opens the chapter's account of the mutual sacrifice-cycle between gods and men (through verse 16) with a founding word to newborn creation: saha-yajñāḥ, 'together with sacrifice', casts humanity as created already bound to yajña as its means of flourishing. Iṣṭa-kāma-dhuk, 'the yielder of desired things', echoes the mythic kāmadhenu, the wish-fulfilling cow, casting sacrifice itself in that role.
#11
L: The-gods nourish by-this [sacrifice]; let-those gods nourish you [in return]; mutually nourishing, the-supreme good you-shall-attain.
I: Nourish the gods with this, and may the gods in turn nourish you; nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good.
N: The reciprocal cycle stated directly: bhāvayata ... bhāvayantu, 'nourish ... let them nourish', the same causative verb used for both directions, presents sacrifice as mutual sustenance between gods and men, not a one-way payment. Parasparam bhāvayantaḥ, 'nourishing one another', generalizes the principle beyond ritual to any relation of mutual care.
#12
L: Desired enjoyments, indeed, to-you the-gods will-give, propitiated-by-sacrifice; by-them given, without-giving-in-return to-them, who enjoys [them] — a-thief indeed he [is].
I: The gods, gratified by sacrifice, will give you the enjoyments you desire. Whoever enjoys their gifts without giving anything back to them is nothing but a thief.
N: The cycle of verse 11 restated as an ethical claim: dattān apradāya, 'having received without giving [anything] in return', names the one who takes the gods' gifts (the natural bounty of rain and harvest, per verse 14) without offering sacrifice back — stenaḥ, 'a thief', a blunt word for what elsewhere might be softened as mere ingratitude.
#13
L: Eaters-of-the-remnants-of-sacrifice, being, are-freed from-all-sins; but the-wicked eat sin, who cook for-their-own-sake.
I: Those who eat what remains after sacrifice are freed from all their faults; but those wicked people who cook only for themselves eat nothing but sin.
N: Yajña-śiṣṭa, 'what remains after sacrifice', names the practice of eating only after offering food first — the same discipline of unattached action, now given a concrete, domestic form. Pacanti ātma-kāraṇāt, 'cook for their own sake alone', is the plain opposite, and agham bhuñjate, 'eat sin', turns the very act of eating into a moral verdict.
#14
L: From-food come-to-be beings; from-rain [is] the-arising-of-food; from-sacrifice arises rain; sacrifice [is] arisen-from-action.
I: Beings arise from food; food is produced from rain; rain arises from sacrifice; and sacrifice arises from action.
N: A chain of dependence traced one step further back from verse 12's simple exchange: bhūtāni-anna-parjanya-yajña-karma, each said to bhavati, 'arise', from the one before — grounding the whole natural order in ritual action, and ritual action in turn in ordinary karma (deliberate human activity), traced one step further still in the next verse.
#15
L: Action, arisen-from-brahman, know; brahman, arisen-from-the-imperishable. Therefore the-all-pervading brahman, eternal, in-sacrifice [is] established.
I: Know that action arises from brahman, and that brahman arises from the imperishable. Therefore brahman, which pervades all things, is always grounded in sacrifice.
N: The chain from verse 14 now reaches brahman (kept untranslated per convention), traced back in turn to akṣara, 'the imperishable' — a still more fundamental reality, named here for the first time and taken up again at 8.3. The verse closes the causal chain begun at verse 9 by folding it back into sacrifice itself: sarva-gataṃ brahma ... yajñe pratiṣṭhitam, 'brahman, all-pervading, is grounded in sacrifice'. This is a hard verse to render literally: ब्रह्माक्षरसमुद्भवम् fuses two words, brahma (accusative, a second object of viddhi) and akṣara-samudbhavam. The word brahma shifts sense within the verse: Śaṅkara glosses the first occurrence (karma brahmodbhavam) specifically as the Veda — action arises from Vedic injunction — distinct from the cosmic, all-pervading brahman of the second line.
#16
L: Thus set-in-motion, the-wheel, who does-not-keep-turning here — sinful-of-life, delighting-in-the-senses, in-vain, O Pārtha, he lives.
I: Whoever, Pārtha, does not keep this wheel turning as it has been set in motion, living a life of sin and delighting only in his senses, lives in vain.
N: Cakra, 'the wheel' (of the sacrifice-cycle just described, verses 9-15), gives the chapter's teaching on sacrifice its closing image and warning: not to keep it turning (na anuvartayati) is named aghāyuḥ, 'living a life of sin' — the mirror image of the yajña-śiṣṭāśinaḥ of verse 13, who are freed from sin. Indriya-ārāmaḥ, 'delighting in the senses', names the private self-indulgence the sacrifice-cycle is meant to counter.
#17
L: But-whoever, delighting-in-the-self alone, might-be, and satisfied-in-the-self, a-man — content in-the-self-alone — for-him a-duty not exists.
I: But the man who finds his delight in the self alone, who is satisfied in the self and content in the self alone — for him there is nothing left to do.
N: A limiting case introduced by yas tu, 'but whoever': the man who has actually reached ātma-rati, 'delight in the self' (a state, not merely a claim, as verse 18 stresses), genuinely has no kāryam, 'nothing that must be done'. This qualifies, rather than contradicts, verses 4-16, since such a man is exceedingly rare, and Arjuna — as the verses that follow make clear — is not yet him.
#18
L: Not-at-all for-him, by-what's-done, [is-there] purpose; nor by-what's-not-done, here, any [purpose] whatsoever; and-not his, among-all-beings, any reliance-for-interest [exists].
I: For such a man, nothing depends on what he does, and nothing depends on what he leaves undone; he has no stake at all, among any being, in anything for his own sake.
N: This spells out what 'nothing to do' (kāryam, verse 17) actually means: not indifference to action itself, but the absence of artha, 'personal interest, purpose', in either doing (kṛtena) or not doing (akṛtena) — and no artha-vyapāśrayaḥ, 'reliance for [his own] interest', on any being. This is the standard the rest of the chapter, from verse 19, asks Arjuna to imitate even without yet having attained it.
#19
L: Therefore, unattached, always, the-action-that-is-to-be-done, perform! Unattached, indeed, performing action, the-supreme attains, a-man.
I: Therefore, always perform the action that must be done, without attachment; for a man who acts without attachment attains the highest goal.
N: The chapter's practical conclusion so far, restating verse 9's asaktaḥ ... samācara almost verbatim, now generalized past sacrifice to kāryaṃ karma, 'action that is [one's] duty' at large. Param āpnoti, 'attains the supreme', names the reward directly — the same word used at verse 15 of brahman's ultimate source, now naming the goal for the man who acts unattached.
#20
L: By-action-alone, indeed, perfection attained, Janaka-and-others; the-welfare-of-the-world alone, indeed, even, considering, to-do you-ought.
I: It was by action alone that Janaka and others attained perfection. You too should act, with an eye only to the world's welfare.
N: Janaka, the legendary philosopher-king of Videha, famed in later tradition as one who ruled and acted while fully liberated, is offered as precedent: karmaṇā eva, 'by action alone' (not by abstaining), he reached saṃsiddhi, 'complete perfection'. Loka-saṃgraha, 'the holding-together of the world, the world's welfare', names for the first time the positive motive the chapter offers Arjuna in place of both personal gain and mere duty, developed through verse 26 and echoed again as Kṛṣṇa's own reason for acting in verses 22-24.
#21
L: Whatever the-best-man does, that very-thing, indeed, the-ordinary person [does]; whatever standard he makes, the-world/people follow that.
I: Whatever a great man does, ordinary people do as well; whatever standard he sets, the world follows it.
N: A second precedent-argument follows Janaka's example directly: śreṣṭhaḥ, 'the best/most excellent [man]', sets pramāṇam, 'the standard, the measure', that itaraḥ janaḥ, 'the ordinary person', imitates — this is the general principle behind loka-saṃgraha (verse 20), and the reason a wise man's unattached action matters beyond himself.
#22
L: Not for-me, O Pārtha, there-is a-duty-to-be-done, in-the-three worlds, anything [whatsoever] — nothing-unobtained-to-be-obtained — [yet] I-remain-engaged, indeed, and, in-action.
I: There is nothing at all in the three worlds, Pārtha, that I must do, nothing unattained that I need attain — and yet I go on acting.
N: Kṛṣṇa now gives his own case as the ultimate instance of verses 20-21's principle: precisely because he has nothing left to gain (nānavāptam avāptavyam, 'nothing unattained to be attained'), his continued action can only be for loka-saṃgraha, the world's sake, developed through verse 24. Varta here is varte, 'I remain engaged' (vṛt), its final -e reduced to -a before the following eva.
#23
L: If, indeed, I not might-be-engaged, ever, in-action, untiring — my path they-follow, men, O Pārtha, in-every-way.
I: For if I were not to keep acting, untiringly, at all times, Pārtha, people would follow my path in every way.
N: A conditional continuing from verse 22: Kṛṣṇa's own ceasing to act — as the ultimate śreṣṭhaḥ of verse 21 — would not be neutral but actively destructive, since manuṣyāḥ ... anuvartante, 'men follow', whatever standard he sets; the consequence is spelled out concretely in the next verse.
#24
L: Would-perish these worlds, if not I-might-do action, if I; of-confusion and a-doer I-might-be; I-might-destroy these creatures.
I: If I did not act, these worlds would collapse; I would be the cause of chaos, and I would destroy all these creatures.
N: The concrete consequence of verse 23's hypothesis: saṃkara, 'confusion, intermingling' (a term used elsewhere of the mixing of social classes, treated by later tradition as a great social evil, e.g. 1.41-43), and the destruction of prajāḥ, 'creatures, subjects' — the stakes of a great man's example (verse 21) taken to their limit.
#25
L: Attached, in-action, the-unwise, just-as act, O Bhārata; should-act, the-wise-man, likewise, unattached, desiring-to-promote the-welfare-of-the-world.
I: Just as the ignorant act with attachment to their work, Bhārata, so the wise man should act without attachment, wishing to uphold the welfare of the world.
N: Loka-saṃgraha, 'the world's welfare' (already named at verse 20), returns as the wise man's explicit motive — the positive answer to the question implicit since verse 17: if the truly wise have nothing left to gain, why should they act at all? Cikīrṣuḥ, 'desiring to do, wishing to promote' (a desiderative formation from kṛ), marks this as deliberate, chosen action, not passive drift.
#26
L: Not a-disturbance-of-understanding should-he-cause, of-the-ignorant, attached-to-action; should-encourage-in all-actions, the-wise-man, disciplined, performing [them himself].
I: Let the wise man not disturb the minds of the ignorant who are attached to their work; disciplined himself, and acting, let him encourage them in all their actions.
N: This states the wise man's social responsibility directly: buddhi-bhedam, 'a splitting of understanding', would only confuse ajñānāṃ karma-saṅginām, 'the ignorant who are attached to action', if suddenly told the truth of verses 17-18 (that action ultimately does not matter to the wise). Joṣayet, 'should encourage [them] to delight in', urges the wise man instead to keep performing action visibly himself (samācaran) as an example, per verses 20-21, rather than preach detachment to those not ready for it.
#27
L: By-nature, being-done, by-the-guṇas, actions, in-every-way; whose-self-is-deluded-by-egoism, '[the] doer I [am]' — thus thinks.
I: Actions are, in every way, performed by the guṇas of nature; but a man whose mind is confused by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer.'
N: The chapter's first extended treatment of the guṇas (kept untranslated per convention; named individually only from chapter 14 on) as the true agents of all action, in contrast to ahaṃkāra, 'egoism' ('the I-maker'), which falsely claims agency for the self. Kartāham iti manyate, '[he] thinks, "I am the doer"', names precisely the error the next two verses correct.
#28
L: But-the-knower-of-the-truth, O mighty-armed-one, regarding-the-distinction-between-the-guṇas-and-their-actions, 'the-guṇas upon-the-guṇas act' — thus having-considered, not he-clings.
I: But the man who knows the truth about the guṇas and their actions, mighty-armed one, thinking 'the guṇas merely act upon the guṇas,' does not become attached.
N: The corrective to verse 27's error: tattva-vit, 'the knower of the truth' (about guṇa-karma-vibhāga, 'the distinction between the guṇas and their actions', i.e. that guṇas act on guṇas, not the self on anything), reaches na sajjate, 'does not cling', exactly by seeing the mechanism verse 27 described — knowledge itself, not extra effort, is what removes attachment.
#29
L: Deluded-by-the-guṇas of-nature, they-cling to-the-actions-of-the-guṇas; those of-incomplete-knowledge, the-dull, one-of-complete-knowledge should-not-unsettle.
I: Those deluded by the guṇas of nature cling to what the guṇas do; but let the man of complete knowledge not unsettle those of partial understanding, the slow-witted.
N: This closes the section begun at verse 26 with the same instruction restated in the guṇa-vocabulary just introduced: akṛtsna-vidaḥ, 'those of incomplete knowledge' — the same ajñānām, 'the ignorant', of verse 26 — should not be vicālayet, 'made to waver', by a kṛtsna-vit, 'one of complete knowledge', showing off what they are not ready to hear.
#30
L: In-me all actions having-laid-down, with-a-mind-fixed-on-the-self, free-from-desire, free-from-mine-ness, having-become, fight! — free-from-anguish.
I: Surrendering all your actions to me, with your mind fixed on the self, free from desire and free from any sense of 'mine,' fight — and be free of anguish.
N: The section on action opened at verse 4 closes with a command directed at Arjuna himself, echoing the house rendering of 2.47 on acting without craving for the fruit: mayi ... saṃnyasya, 'having surrendered all actions in me', anticipates the fuller teaching on surrender to Kṛṣṇa personally that develops from chapter 7 on. Vigata-jvaraḥ, 'free from the fever [of anguish]', gives that anguish a vivid, almost physical name.
#31
L: Who my this doctrine constantly follow, men, faithful, uncomplaining — they too are-freed from-actions.
I: Those who constantly follow this teaching of mine, with faith and without envy — they too are freed from the bondage of action.
N: The teaching just given (verses 4-30) is now offered its own reward, addressed to any follower, not only Arjuna: śraddhāvantaḥ, 'possessed of faith', and anasūyantaḥ, 'free from envy, fault-finding', are the two qualities required; mucyante ... karmabhiḥ, 'are freed from actions', recalls karma-bandhanaḥ, 'bound by action', from verse 9.
#32
L: But-who, this finding-fault-with, do-not follow my doctrine — deluded-in-all-knowledge, those, know! lost, senseless.
I: But those who find fault with this teaching and do not follow it — know them to be blind to all wisdom, lost, and without understanding.
N: The negative counterpart to verse 31: abhyasūyantaḥ, 'finding fault, carping' (the opposite of verse 31's anasūyantaḥ), leads not merely to missing a benefit but to naṣṭān acetasaḥ, 'lost, senseless' — the chapter's harshest judgment on the willfully resistant listener.
#33
L: In-accordance-with acts, his-own nature, even-the-learned-man; nature follow, beings; restraint what will-accomplish?
I: Even a man of knowledge acts according to his own nature; all beings follow their nature — what good is forcible restraint?
N: A candid limit on the teaching just given (verses 27-29): jñānavān api, 'even the learned/wise man', still acts sadṛśaṃ svasyāḥ prakṛteḥ, 'in accordance with his own nature' — knowledge changes how one relates to action (verse 28), not the underlying nature (prakṛti) itself. Nigrahaḥ, 'forcible restraint, suppression', is shown here to be largely futile against it, setting up verse 34's more targeted advice.
#34
L: For-each-sense, in-its-object, passion-and-aversion [stand] fixed; let-one-not come-under-the-control of-these-two, for-these-two, indeed, [are] his two-waylayers.
I: Passion and aversion are fixed toward the objects of each sense; one should not come under the sway of these two, for they lie in ambush as one's true enemies.
N: The targeted advice that follows from verse 33's admission that total suppression is futile: rāga and dveṣa, 'passion (attraction) and aversion' (ordinary vocabulary, not among the untranslated terms), are what actually need controlling, sense by sense, rather than the senses' contact with objects as such. Paripanthinau, 'the two who lie in wait on the road', a vivid image of ambush, names them as enemies more dangerous than any external one, anticipating verse 37's identification of the real enemy.
#35
L: Better, one's-own-dharma, deficient, than-another's-dharma well-performed; in-one's-own-dharma, death, [is] better — another's-dharma [is] danger-bringing.
I: It is better to do one's own dharma imperfectly than another's well; death while doing one's own dharma is better — another's dharma is fraught with danger.
N: The chapter's summary maxim on sva-dharma (already named in substance at verse 8, and taken up again at 18.47 near the poem's close). Dharma here is explicitly relative to the person: para-dharma, 'another's dharma' (a duty not one's own by class and station), is bhaya-āvahaḥ, 'danger-bringing', however well performed, because it is not truly one's own. Sva-dharma is left untranslated per convention, in the personal-duty sense of dharma rather than the cosmic-order sense used elsewhere.
#36
L: Now, by-what, impelled, this — sin does-commit, a-man, unwilling, even, O descendant-of-Vṛṣṇi — by-force, as-it-were, compelled?
I: Arjuna said: Then what is it, Vārṣṇeya, that impels a man to commit sin, even against his will, as if driven to it by force?
N: A new question opens the chapter's final movement: Arjuna picks up the language of verses 27 and 33-34 (being driven by something other than one's own choice) and asks directly what that something is. Vārṣṇeya, 'descendant of Vṛṣṇi' (Kṛṣṇa's clan), is a new epithet of Kṛṣṇa in this chapter; balād iva niyojitaḥ, 'as if compelled by force', anticipates Kṛṣṇa's answer at verse 37 — not literal external compulsion, but something that feels like it.
#37
L: Desire, this; anger, this — arisen-from-the-guṇa-rajas; great-devourer, greatly-sinful — know it, here, [as] the-enemy.
I: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the guṇa rajas — insatiable and deeply sinful; know this to be the enemy here.
N: Kṛṣṇa's answer identifies the force behind verse 36's 'as if compelled by force' precisely: kāma, 'desire', which shows itself as krodha, 'anger', is traced to rajo-guṇa, 'the guṇa rajas' (the second of the three guṇas, named individually here for the first time, though still untranslated per convention and only formally defined in chapter 14). Vairiṇam, 'the enemy', gives concrete shape to the paripanthinau, 'the two waylayers', of verse 34. This is among the poem's most quoted lines, the companion, several chapters on, to 16.21's 'triple gate to hell' (kāma, krodha, lobha); its doubled kāma eṣaḥ krodha eṣaḥ shows the same irregularity already met in sa/saḥ (e.g. verse 6 above, and chapters 1-2): eṣaḥ, like sa, drops its visarga before any following consonant rather than converting it in the usual way.
#38
L: By-smoke is-covered fire, just-as a-mirror by-dust; just-as by-the-caul covered [is] the-embryo, so by-that this [is] covered.
I: As fire is veiled by smoke and a mirror by dust, and as an embryo is covered by its caul, so is this covered by that.
N: Three similes in ascending order of how deeply the covering hides what it covers — smoke over fire (removable at a touch), dust over a mirror (needing a wipe), the caul over an embryo (an organic, inseparable covering). The verse deliberately leaves 'this' (idam) and 'that' (tena) unnamed; only verse 39 identifies them as jñānam, 'knowledge', and kāma, 'desire' — a suspense the translation preserves rather than resolving early.
#39
L: Covered, [is] knowledge, by-this, of-the-knower, by-[his]-constant-enemy — in-the-form-of-desire, O son-of-Kuntī, insatiable, like-a-fire.
I: The wise man's knowledge is veiled by this, its constant enemy in the shape of desire — a fire, Kaunteya, that is never filled.
N: The chapter's central identification, resolving verse 38's riddle: kāma-rūpeṇa, 'in the form of desire', names what covers jñāna, while duṣpūreṇa analena, 'an insatiable fire', gives desire two more images at once — never satisfied (pūra, 'filling') and consuming (anala, 'fire'), the same fire-image already used literally in verse 38's first simile.
#40
L: The-senses, the-mind, the-understanding — its seat, is-called; by-these, deludes, this [enemy], knowledge having-covered, the-embodied-one.
I: The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be desire's seat; through these it deludes the embodied self, veiling its knowledge.
N: The chain of faculties — indriyāṇi, manaḥ, buddhiḥ, 'the senses, the mind, the understanding' — is named here as kāma's adhiṣṭhānam, 'seat, base of operations', in ascending order (the same hierarchy verse 42 restates as a ranking of what is 'higher'); this diagnostic verse prepares the practical instruction of verse 41.
#41
L: Therefore, you, the-senses, at-the-outset, having-restrained, O bull-among-the-Bharatas — the-evil-thing strike-down, indeed, this, the-destroyer-of-knowledge-and-discernment.
I: Therefore, bull among the Bharatas, first restrain your senses, and strike down this evil thing that destroys both knowledge and discernment.
N: The command answering verse 36's question directly: niyamya, 'having restrained' (the senses, the first and outermost of the three faculties named in verse 40), is the starting point, but the real target is pāpmānam ... jñāna-vijñāna-nāśanam, 'the sinful destroyer of knowledge and discernment', i.e. kāma itself — jñāna and vijñāna together (ordinary knowledge and its more discriminating, applied form) name everything desire is said to ruin.
#42
L: The-senses, higher, they-say, than-the-senses higher, the-mind; than-the-mind, but, higher, understanding; who than-understanding higher, but, he [is].
I: The senses, they say, are higher than their objects; the mind is higher than the senses; understanding is higher than the mind; and higher still than understanding is he, the self.
N: The hierarchy of verse 40 (senses, mind, understanding) is extended one rung further, with each successive term said to be para, 'higher, beyond' the one before: indriya < manas < buddhi < the self (referred to only as saḥ, 'he', not named ātman here, though that is what tradition understands). This ladder is the basis for verse 43's final instruction: since the self stands above understanding, it alone has the standing to master what lies below it.
#43
L: Thus, than-understanding, that-which-is-higher having-known, having-steadied the-self by-the-self — slay! the-enemy, O mighty-armed-one, having-the-form-of-desire, hard-to-overcome.
I: So, knowing that which stands higher than understanding, and steadying the self by the self, slay this enemy in the form of desire, mighty-armed one — hard as it is to overcome.
N: The chapter closes on the practical command anticipated by verse 42's hierarchy: buddheḥ param, 'that which is higher than understanding' (i.e. the self, ātman), once known (buddhvā), gives one the standing to accomplish ātmānam ātmanā saṃstabhya, 'steadying the self by the self' — a phrase whose apparent circularity states precisely that the higher self must master the lower, psychological one. Durāsadam, 'hard to approach, hard to overcome', is the chapter's last word of respect for the enemy it has spent its final movement (verses 34-43) exposing and commanding Arjuna to destroy.
